✅ HSRP failover follows this sequence: the active router fails; the standby stops receiving hello messages; the standby takes the active role; the new active assumes the virtual IP and MAC. Hosts keep using the same gateway.
💡 Failure → missing hellos → takeover → virtual addresses.

1) Start with the question: Start with the host’s view: it needs a stable default gateway even when one router fails. A first-hop redundancy group supplies a virtual gateway, backed by multiple physical routers. The host uses the virtual IP and the associated virtual MAC.
2) Work through it: For HSRP, identify the active router that forwards and the elected standby that is ready to replace it. Higher priority is preferred; preemption allows an eligible higher-priority router to reclaim the active role. Default hello/hold timers are three and ten seconds unless configured otherwise.

1) Start with the question: Decide whether the device is a client, server or relay. A new IPv4 client initially lacks a usable address and may not know a DHCP server. The server leases an address with configuration such as the mask, gateway and DNS servers.

3) Apply the distinction: Check the layer named in the question. The IPv4 limited broadcast is 255.255.255.255; the Ethernet broadcast is FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF. DHCP uses UDP server port 67 and client port 68. A relay forwards client requests between subnets because routers do not normally forward local broadcasts.

1) Start with the question: Separate coverage from capacity. Coverage asks whether the signal reaches a location reliably; capacity asks how much useful traffic the shared radio channel can carry. A stronger signal does not remove every source of contention or interference.

1) Start with the question: Classify the network by its intended geographic scope, rather than by the presence of radio alone. Personal, local, metropolitan and wide-area networks can all be wireless, but they support different kinds of coverage.
